# Task A1 – Design the Data Acquisition (K3)

**Files:** `TaskA1/design.md` (this text), `schema.sql`, `inspect_source.py`, `compare_csv_vs_sql.py`; data generated by `data/generate_data.py`.

## A1.1 Inspect the source
The 12 stations send one CSV file a day (`<station>_<YYYY-MM-DD>.csv`; October 2026: 372 files, 8,966 data rows). The station is named in the **file name**; the file has the header `date,hour,pm25,pm10,no2,temp` and one line per hour: date, hour 0–23, PM2.5, PM10 and NO₂ in µg/m³, temperature. The data are generated by `generate_data.py`, which injects the problems described in the case study; `inspect_source.py` then counts them:
```text

blank value                            731   adyar_2026-10-01.csv line 10: 2026-10-01,8,65.6,,,27.1
'NA' value                             508   adyar_2026-10-01.csv line 2: 2026-10-01,0,54.8,84.7,NA,26.2
negative pollutant value               110   adyar_2026-10-04.csv line 5: 2026-10-04,3,30.2,-37.3,45.8,21.3

   kodungaiyur      80.0   <-- Fahrenheit
   anna_nagar       26.7

```

| Problem | Example (from the files) | Consequence if ignored |
|---|---|---|
| blank value | `2026-10-01,8,65.6,,,27.1` | the reading is not a number; `float("")` stops the program |
| `NA` / `ERR` / `--` | `…,54.8,84.7,NA,26.2` | same; the text must be recognised as "missing" |
| negative value | `…,30.2,-37.3,45.8,…` | a concentration cannot be negative; it would pull the average down |
| impossibly large value | `…,58.6,104.3,999.9,…` | sensor fault; would dominate means and charts |
| duplicate row | the same date and hour twice | the hour is counted twice |
| hour 24 | `2026-10-29,24,54.9,…` | hours are 0–23 |
| date in another format | `01/10/2026,0,42.8,…` (T Nagar) | dates would not sort or group correctly |
| Fahrenheit temperatures | Velachery and Kodungaiyur: mean 80, not 27 | temperature in the wrong unit makes charts and correlation meaningless |
| station name only in the file name | `t_nagar_…` | the name must be mapped to a standard name and id |

## A1.2 Design the storage (SQLite)
```sql
stations(station_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE, latitude REAL, longitude REAL, temp_unit TEXT CHECK in ('C','F'))
readings(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, station_id TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES stations, day TEXT NOT NULL, hour INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK 0..23,
         pm25 REAL, pm10 REAL, no2 REAL, temp_c REAL)       -- CHECK constraints keep every value inside its valid range
```
(complete statements in `schema.sql`). **Mapping:** the file name gives `station_id` (through `stations.name`); CSV `date` → `day` (ISO text, SQLite has no date type); `hour` → `hour`; `pm25`, `pm10`, `no2` → the same names in µg/m³; `temp` → `temp_c` (always Celsius: the Fahrenheit values are converted before storing, and `stations.temp_unit` remembers what the station reports). A missing or invalid reading becomes `NULL`, not 0, so that `AVG()` and `COUNT()` ignore it. **Keys:** `stations.station_id` is the natural primary key; `readings.id` is a surrogate key, because the real identity of a reading is (station, day, hour) and that rule is enforced by the cleaning step (duplicates are removed); a `UNIQUE(station_id, day, hour)` index is recommended for production and is evaluated in B4.2.

## A1.3 CSV or SQL?
Three typical questions of the board: **(1)** the average PM2.5 of one station in October, **(2)** the stations with the highest monthly mean, **(3)** the number of days each station exceeded the daily limit of 60 µg/m³.

| Question | From the CSV files | With SQL |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | open and parse every file, keep the lines of one station and month, add them up (about 6 lines) | `SELECT AVG(pm25) FROM readings JOIN stations … WHERE name=? AND day BETWEEN …` |
| 2 | dictionary of lists per station, mean of each, sort (about 5 lines) | `… GROUP BY name ORDER BY AVG(pm25) DESC LIMIT 3` |
| 3 | dictionary of lists per (station, day), mean, count above 60 (about 6 lines) | a sub-query `GROUP BY station_id, day`, then `WHERE daily > 60 GROUP BY name` |

The CSV method **re-reads and re-parses all the files for every question**, the code is longer and each question has a new set of loops, and the rules of the data (valid ranges, one row per hour) are not enforced anywhere. SQL reads data that is already clean and typed, states *what* is wanted instead of *how*, can use an index, and the database enforces the rules with its constraints. The CSV files remain the right format for *exchange* and *archive*; the database is the right format for *questions*. B1.3 answers all three with both methods; the results agree.

## Alternative – everything in CSV and a pandas DataFrame loaded for each question
```
FOR EACH question DO
    df <- READ_CSV(whole file)            O(n) time, O(n) memory
    result <- FILTER and AGGREGATE df     O(n)
```
```text
stations       rows |  pandas: read CSV + filter  SQL scan (no index)  SQL with index |  CSV on disk  DB on disk  DataFrame in RAM | same answer
      12    105,120 |                    0.071 s              5.76 ms        0.182 ms |       4.2 MB      8.7 MB           16.0 MB | True
     120  1,051,200 |                    0.584 s             51.72 ms        0.190 ms |      42.4 MB     87.9 MB          159.8 MB | True
query plan with index: SEARCH readings USING INDEX idx_station_day (station_id=? AND day>? AND day<?)
```

| Stations / rows | pandas: read CSV + filter | SQL, full scan | SQL, index on (station_id, day) | CSV | database | DataFrame in RAM |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 12 / 105,120 | 0.071 s | 5.8 ms | 0.18 ms | 4.2 MB | 8.7 MB | 16.0 MB |
| 120 / 1,051,200 | 0.584 s | 51.7 ms | 0.19 ms | 42.4 MB | 87.9 MB | 159.8 MB |

**Time per question:** pandas has to read all n rows every time – O(n); with 10× more data it took 8× longer. SQLite without an index also scans (O(n)) but reads its own compact binary format (10× faster than parsing text); with an index on (station_id, day) the query is a B-tree search, **O(log n + k)** for the k matching rows: 0.18 ms → 0.19 ms when the data grew 10× (the plan shows `SEARCH … USING INDEX`). **Space:** the CSV is the smallest file on disk (4.2 MB against 8.7 MB, because the database also stores the key, types and the index structure), but the DataFrame needs about 16 MB of **memory** for the same rows – memory grows with the data for every question, whereas SQLite keeps the data on disk and reads only the pages it needs. The pandas answer would be preferable only for a quick one-off look at one file.
